1.sense: A command to report, not to argue. What the Prophet ﷺ knows of that night's audience he knows by revelation: a small party of jinn stopped, listened, and went back to their people with a verdict. Their word for what they heard is ʿajab, the thing there is no precedent to measure against.

notes.t: Nafar is a small band, few enough to be counted by eye; the lexicographers put it between three and ten. The surah opens on a handful, not a crowd.

Ibn ʿAbbas reports that the Prophet ﷺ was travelling toward the market of ʿUkaz and led the dawn prayer at Nakhla, and that jinn passing by heard the recitation. He did not see them and did not recite to them; he learned of it when this surah came down, which is why the verse begins with a report of revelation.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Ibn ʿAbbas

notes.t: The same night is told from the other side in Al-Ahqaf, where a company of jinn is turned toward the recitation and then goes back to warn their own people.

links.why: what the jinn are made of, a flame without smoke

2.sense: The verdict has two halves: what the recitation does, and what the hearers will do about it. Rushd is the soundness of judgment that keeps a traveller on his road. The first conclusion they draw from a book heard once is that nothing will be set beside its Author.

notes.t: The root r-sh-d runs through the surah: rushd here, rashad at verses 10, 14 and 21. It is the word the passage keeps returning to, and it is what the jinn say the recitation supplies.
Rushd is set against ghayy, the wandering off the path, in the verse that says the two have become distinct.

links.why: the same verdict in their own words to their people, a book guiding to the truth
rashad asked for as a gift by the young men of the cave

3.sense: The denial follows the order in which a family is built: no wife, and so no son. Jadd is greatness, the standing a person carries, and the verb lifts it clear above the claim being denied. The speakers are unmaking something said about themselves as well, since the Arabs had drawn a lineage between Allah and the jinn.

notes.t: The Qur'an argues in the same order and with the same word, asking how He should have a child when He has had no consort.

Jadd also means fortune or wealth, and it carries that sense in the words the Prophet ﷺ said after the prayer: no withholder of what You give, and the fortune of the man of fortune does not avail him against You.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from al-Mughira ibn Shuʿba

notes.t: The reciters and commentators differ over the vowel on the particle that opens most of the verses from here to 14. Read with a fatha it continues the report, that it has been revealed to me that such and such; read with a kasra it is fresh direct speech from the jinn. The passage carries either way.
notes.src: the difference is recorded among the standard readings and set out by the commentators

links.why: the lineage the Arabs invented between Allah and the jinn, which this sentence cancels
the same denial with no consort mentioned, stripped to the verb

4.sense: A wrong reported from inside their own community. Safīh is the light-minded one whose judgment carries no weight; shaṭaṭ is speech that has gone past the far bank and kept going. Kana with the imperfect makes it a settled habit rather than one slip.

notes.t: The root sh-ṭ-ṭ gives shaṭṭ, the bank of a river, and the noun here is the going beyond a limit. What is described is not error but overshoot.
The commentators divide over who the foolish one is: Iblis in particular, or the reckless among the jinn taken generally. Both are recorded.
The claim that Allah has taken a child is called, elsewhere, a grave word coming out of their mouths, which is the register shaṭaṭ belongs to.

links.why: Iblis named as one of the jinn, and what he did with the command

5.sense: What let the falsehood in was a presumption of honesty. Neither kind, they had assumed, would put a lie in Allah's mouth, so what they were told about Him they took on trust. The recitation is what broke the assumption.

notes.t: Ẓann here is a working assumption held without checking, not a doubt. The verb returns at verses 7 and 12, once for a judgment that turned out false and once for one that held.
The Qur'an puts inventing a lie about Allah at the head of its list of wrongs, asking who is more unjust than the one who does it.

links.why: what becomes of those who do invent against Allah

6.sense: The commentators report the custom behind the line: a man halting in a valley at nightfall would say he took refuge with the master of that valley. The verse describes the return on that transaction. Rahaq is what settles over a man and weighs on him, and the arrangement produced more of it.

notes.t: The verb rahiqa is used of dust or darkness settling over a face, and of a debt overtaking its owner. The word returns at verse 13, where the believer is told he need not fear it.
The commentators divide over who gained the rahaq: the jinn adding to the burden of the men who came to them, or the men adding to the insolence of the jinn by treating them as protectors.
The Qur'an stages the reckoning for this traffic, with the human allies of the jinn admitting that each kind had made use of the other.

links.why: the angels on the Day: it was the jinn most of them were believing in

7.sense: The speakers turn to their own audience and put them in the same sentence as the humans. One error is held on both sides of the partition between the two kinds. Baʿth is the raising of a body from the ground and also the sending out of a messenger.

notes.t: The only second person inside the jinn's speech. They are addressing their own people, and the pronoun makes the charge local before it is general.
The commentators read yabʿatha two ways, that Allah would raise no one from the dead and that He would send no one as a messenger. Both are recorded, and the surah has use for each.
The same denial is quoted and answered directly elsewhere: they claim they will never be raised, and the reply is an oath that they will.

links.why: the oath the deniers swore that Allah will not raise the one who dies

8.sense: Lams is feeling for a thing with the hand, the way a man searches in the dark. They went up on the usual errand and found the sky under garrison. The guard is described as a fullness rather than a wall: there is no gap left to slip through.

notes.t: A shihab is a brand of fire pulled from a blaze, which is how the streak across the sky gets its name. The word is concrete before it is astronomical.
The sky is described as guarded against every rebellious devil, who cannot listen in to the highest assembly and is pelted from every side.

links.why: the lamps of the nearest sky doubling as missiles
the one who snatches a hearing and the clear flame that follows him

9.sense: An old routine and its cancellation in one breath. They had stations up there, places kept for eavesdropping, and the verb is the habitual one. Raṣad is a watch posted to wait for a particular arrival, so the seat the listener used to take is now occupied by what is waiting for him.

notes.t: Maqʿad is a place of sitting and raṣad is an ambush laid for a man's coming. The two words put the same spot to two uses one line apart.
The Qur'an says of itself that the devils did not bring it down and could not, since they are held off from the hearing.
ʿAʾisha reports the Prophet ﷺ describing what the fortune-tellers work from: a word snatched from above and carried down, to which a hundred lies are added.

links.why: the same word raṣad at the surah's end, a guard set to protect a revelation rather than to intercept one

10.sense: Something has changed in the sky and the jinn cannot read it. The two possibilities are put in unequal grammar: the evil is intended by nobody named, the guidance is intended by their Lord, who is named. Their ignorance is stated plainly, and the surah returns to that ignorance at the end.

notes.t: Evil is left in the passive with no agent attached; the good is put in the active with the Lord as its author. The asymmetry is the manners of the sentence, not a gap in it.
Ibrahim speaks the same way when he lists what his Lord does for him: when I am ill, He cures me. The illness is not ascribed, the healing is.
The verb darā, to know a thing by picking it up, recurs at verse 25, where the same admission is made by the Prophet ﷺ on command.

links.why: the jinn's ignorance of the unseen shown by a dead king still leaning on his staff

11.sense: The jinn describe their own society without flattering it. Ṭarāʾiq are roads or ways; qidad are strips cut lengthwise from a hide, each one whole and none of them the same piece. What is claimed is variety, not innocence, and it sets up the sorting at verse 14.

notes.t: Qadda is to split a thing along its length, as against qaṭṭa, to cut across it. A qidda is the strip that comes off. The community is described as one hide gone into ribbons.
The same verb is used of a shirt torn from behind, which is the physical picture the plural here is built on.
Dūna dhālika, below that, is a courtesy. The speakers name the good among them and leave the rest described only by position.

links.why: the same fracturing described of human communities, each faction pleased with its own piece

12.sense: The one assumption of theirs that held. Iʿjāz is leaving a pursuer helpless, being the one who gets away, and they deny they can manage it. Ground and flight cover the two exits a creature with their reputation might reach for.

notes.t: Haraban is an accusative of manner, by way of running. The verb is repeated rather than extended, so the second denial closes a second door instead of restating the first.
The jinn in Al-Ahqaf tell their people the same thing: whoever does not answer the caller of Allah is not going to escape on the earth.
Both kinds are challenged to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth if they can, and told they will not except by an authority they do not have.

links.why: the same denial addressed to people, on the earth and in the sky

13.sense: The last of the jinn's own sentences goes back to the night being reported. Bakhs is what is shaved off a price or a wage; rahaq is the weight that settles on a man. One is being given less than is owed and the other is being made to carry more, and the believer is told he faces neither.

notes.t: Bakhs is the docked price, the sum knocked down below worth. It is the word used for what Yusuf was sold for.
The same pair of fears is denied to the believer in Ta Ha in the same construction, injustice on one side and having his due cut short on the other.
Rahaq returns from verse 6, where the men who went to the jinn for protection were given more of it. The jinn close their speech on the very thing their audience had been buying.

links.why: the jinn's call to their people, with forgiveness and safety stated as the terms

14.sense: The sorting the passage has been moving toward. The line is drawn between muslim and qāsiṭ, not between better and worse conduct, so submission is the only cut being made. Taḥarrā is to aim at a thing with care, the verb for a man taking trouble to find an exact direction.

notes.t: Qāsiṭ is one who swerves off; from the same root the fourth form gives muqsiṭ, one who deals evenly. The letter that turns the sense is a prefix.
The Qur'an says of the muqsiṭīn, the ones who deal justly, that Allah loves them, which is the far end of the root from the word used here.
The same verb is used in the instruction to seek out the Night of Decree among the odd nights of the last ten. It is a word for searching with effort, not for stumbling on something.

links.why: the same community sorted a first time, by conduct, before it is sorted here by submission

15.sense: The other half of the sorting, and the sentence is one word long. Ḥaṭab is gathered wood, what is picked up in order to be burned. They are not put into a fire so much as counted as its material, and nothing further is said about them.

notes.t: Ḥaṭab is cut and carried wood; the man who collects it is a ḥaṭṭāb. The image is of a supply already stacked, waiting on a use.
The Fire is described elsewhere by what feeds it, people and stones, so the idea of a creature counted as fuel is not new here.
Those worshipped besides Allah, and those who worshipped them, are together called the kindling of Hell.

links.why: Hell filled from both kinds together, jinn and people

16.sense: The jinn's report is over and the speech turns. Istiqāma is holding a straight line with no drift, and the return named for it is water in quantity, which is the plainest shape wealth takes for people who live off rain. The conditional is contrary to fact.

notes.t: The commentators read the ṭarīqa two ways: the straight way, so the water is a reward, or the way they were already on, so the water is a rope let out. The next verse, which calls it a test, is read in support of either.
notes.src: at-Tabari sets out both; Ibn Kathir reports the same division

notes.t: Nuh, in the surah just before this one, promises his people rain sent down in abundance if they will seek forgiveness.
The Qur'an also describes the doors of every good thing being opened to people who had forgotten, until they were seized while pleased with what they had.

links.why: istiqama named as the whole of the demand, and what descends on those who hold it

17.sense: The water comes with a purpose attached and the purpose is a test. Salaka is to thread a thing into a narrow passage, the verb for putting a cord through the eye of a needle. Ṣaʿad is a climb, so the punishment is described by the effort of it rather than by its heat.

notes.t: The root ṣ-ʿ-d is ascent. The same word appears in Al-Muddaththir as ṣaʿūd, a punishment made of going uphill without arriving.
Turning away from the remembrance of the Lord is met elsewhere with a life pressed narrow, the same consequence in a different image.
Yasluk returns at verse 27, where what is threaded through is a guard set around a messenger. The verb does both jobs in one surah.

links.why: wealth and children extended as no favour at all

18.sense: Masjid is the place where the forehead goes down, and the plural is not confined to buildings. Ownership is stated first and the prohibition follows from it: ground that belongs to one owner is not ground on which to address two. The verb is duʿāʾ, calling on someone, which is what a person does at the moment he is lowest.

notes.t: Among the things the Prophet ﷺ said he had been given was that the earth was made for him a place of prayer and a means of purification, so a masjid is a function of the ground before it is a structure on it.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah

notes.t: The Qur'an joins the same two halves in one line: set your faces at every masjid, and call on Him with the religion made sincerely His.
The commentators also record masājid read as the limbs a body prostrates on, so that the sentence says the parts that touch the ground belong to Allah. The places of prayer is the wider reading.
notes.src: both are recorded in the early tafsir material

links.why: who is fit to keep the masajid of Allah in use

19.sense: The servant of Allah stands and calls on his Lord, and something presses in around him. Libad is matter pressed together, wool matted into felt, a mass with no space left inside it. The scene is given without naming who is crowding.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ is named here by servanthood alone, at the moment he is calling on his Lord, as he is at the opening of Al-Isra, Al-Kahf and An-Najm.
The commentators divide over who nearly piled onto him: the jinn packing in to hear the recitation, or his own people massing against him as he prayed.
The root l-b-d gives the felt-maker's word for wool beaten into a solid sheet, and lubad for wealth heaped up in bulk, as the boaster claims in Al-Balad.

links.why: the plotting his standing provoked, on the second reading of who crowded

20.sense: The reply to the crowd says nothing about the crowd. Innamā fences the verb: one being called on, and no second name admitted beside Him. The words repeat what the jinn said at verse 2, so the report and the answer to it now use the same sentence.

notes.t: Four verses in this closing stretch begin with qul, at 20, 21, 22 and 25. The surah answers a hostile audience entirely in speech that was issued to the Prophet ﷺ rather than composed by him.
The Qur'an ends a surah on the same clause, that the one who hopes to meet his Lord should associate no one in his Lord's worship.

links.why: the same instructed reply to people disputing with him: I was commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him

21.sense: The disclaimer is put in terms of ownership: he does not hold either outcome in hand to give out. Harm is paired not with benefit but with rashad, which fits a surah whose subject is direction. What he does hold is named two verses later, and it is a message.

notes.t: The expected opposite of ḍarr is nafʿ, benefit. Rashad is put in its place, and it is the word the jinn used at verse 2 for what they had found.
The same denial is made about himself: he holds no benefit or harm for his own person except as Allah wills, and had he known the unseen he would have gathered much good.

links.why: the limit stated about himself and his audience together, that he does not know what will be done with either

22.sense: Ijāra is the protection a strong man extends over a weaker one, the standing arrangement of that society, and it is denied here against Allah. Multaḥad is a place to turn aside into; the root gives laḥd, the niche cut into the side of a grave. The Prophet ﷺ is placed under the same terms as everyone he is addressing.

notes.t: The l-ḥ-d root is a turning aside from a straight line, whether into a grave's side niche or away from a name. A multaḥad is somewhere to duck into, not a fortress to hold.
The identical phrase closes a verse in Al-Kahf: there is no changing His words, and you will never find besides Him a place to turn into.
Of Allah it is said that He protects and no one is protected against Him, which is the sentence this verse applies to its speaker.

links.why: the case where protection between people is granted and honoured, so the denial here is about its limit and not its worth

23.sense: The exception names the one thing he does hold: balāgh, the getting of something to where it was sent. Risālāt is plural, so the load is a set of messages rather than one announcement. The warning attached to it is the only place in the surah where a punishment is given a duration.

notes.t: The grammarians differ over what the exception hangs on: the possessing of verse 21, so that delivery is the one thing he owns, or the refuge of verse 22, so that delivery is the only shelter there is.
notes.src: the two constructions are set out in the classical tafsirs and the works on iʿrab

notes.t: The same root carries the command given to the Messenger: deliver what has been sent down to you from your Lord.
The phrase whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger appears in An-Nisa attached to the same outcome, there tied to transgressing the limits He set.

The commentators take the disobedience named here as the rejection the passage has been describing, since the term attached to it is unending. Who abides forever is discussed at length in the tafsirs.
notes.src: the commentators differ on the scope of the verb here

links.why: the messenger's charge stated as delivery and nothing beyond it

24.sense: The sentence runs on from the warning and lands on a comparison, which means the comparison had first been made the other way. Backers and numbers were the argument used against a small community in Mecca. Both terms are settled on the day the promise is seen and not before.

notes.t: The two comparatives name the two things a tribe counted: who stands with you, and how many of you there are. Nothing is said about who is right, only about who was measuring.
The owner of the two gardens makes exactly this boast, that he has more wealth and a mightier band of men.
The disbelievers ask which of the two parties is better in standing and finer in assembly, and the question is the one this verse answers.

links.why: a body of men confident of its own numbers, and what becomes of it

25.sense: The promise just named is left without a date, and the ignorance stated is the Prophet's ﷺ own, said on command. Amad is a stretch of time with a far end fixed to it. The jinn admitted at verse 10 that they could not read what was intended; the same admission is now put in the mouth of the one they had been listening to.

notes.t: Al-Anbiya has the same wording almost exactly: I have announced to you all alike, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far.
When people ask for the hour of the Hour, the answer given is that its knowledge sits with the Lord alone and that it lies heavy on the heavens and the earth.
Amad is a term with a limit at its end, unlike dahr, which is duration without one. What is denied is the date, not the event.

links.why: the same question about the Hour returned to Allah, with only its possible nearness left standing

26.sense: The reason for that ignorance is given as a description of Allah rather than as a limit placed on the Prophet ﷺ. Ghayb is whatever is absent from perception, and calling it His unseen makes it property. Yuẓhiru ʿalā is to put someone above a thing so that he can look down into it.

notes.t: Aḥadan closes verses 2, 7, 18, 20 and 26, and aḥadun stands inside verse 22. The rhyme word of the surah is the word for a single unnamed person, and it does duty for the partner denied and for the knower excluded.
With Him are the keys of the unseen, which no one knows but He.
Al-Imran states the same rule with the same exception: Allah would not disclose the unseen to you, but He chooses from His messengers whom He wills.

links.why: no one in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except Allah

27.sense: The exception is narrow and is not about merit: irtaḍā is Allah's approval and rasūl is an office. What follows describes the delivery under escort, a watch running in front of the messenger and behind him, so that what was sent arrives as it was sent.

notes.t: Min bayni yadayhi is literally from between his hands, the ordinary Arabic for what lies in front of a person. The pair with min khalfihi covers the whole approach.
Raṣad returns from verse 9. There it was a watch waiting to burn an eavesdropper; here it walks with the messenger. One word, and the two ends of a single operation.
The Qur'an describes attendants before a man and behind him who guard him by the command of Allah, the same arrangement in a general case.

links.why: the trustworthy spirit bringing the revelation down, the other half of the escort

28.sense: The escort has a purpose, and the purpose is that the delivery be known to have arrived intact. Aḥāṭa is to surround a thing on every side; aḥṣā is to reckon it item by item. A surah that opened with jinn listening in at the edge of the sky closes with everything counted, them included.

notes.t: The commentators differ over whose knowing liyaʿlama is: the messenger's, that the guard was there and nothing was lost in transit, or Allah's knowledge as it becomes manifest in the event.
notes.src: at-Tabari sets out both, and the later commentators follow him

notes.t: The Qur'an describes the messengers as those who deliver the messages of Allah and fear Him, fearing no one but Him, which is the same verb and the same plural noun.
Everything counted is a formula the Qur'an uses of the record: We have enumerated all things in writing.
ʿAdadan is the last word of the surah and aḥadan was its recurring one. The surah ends on number after spending itself on the One who has no second.

links.why: the same counting, filed in a clear register
